t.6.53.1: Thus addressed, Kumbhakarṇa rebuked Mahodara and then spoke to his brother Rāvaṇa, the foremost of the rākṣasas.
t.6.53.2: I, then, shall today wipe away your dreadful fear by slaying that wicked-souled Rāma; be free of enemies and be happy.
t.6.53.3: Heroes do not roar in vain, like clouds empty of water. Behold now my roar being made good by deeds in battle!
t.6.53.4: He does not indulge himself, nor does he extol himself by his own account; the brave, without making a display of it, accomplish deeds that are hard to do.
t.6.53.5: O Mahodara, such is the way of timid and witless kings who fancy themselves learned, who listen to this from the very outset from the likes of you.
t.6.53.6: This undertaking has been ruined by you, who are ever cowards in battle, speakers of pleasing words, merely following the king's lead.
t.6.53.7: Having come under this king, an enemy who wears the mark of a friend, Laṅkā has been left with only its king remaining; the treasury is drained and the army slain.
t.6.53.8: Here I go forth now to battle, intent on conquering the enemy, to set right today in the great fight the folly of your policy.
t.6.53.9: When the wise Kumbhakarṇa had spoken these words, the lord of the rākṣasas, laughing, then replied to him with these words.
t.6.53.10: This Mahodara is terrified of Rāma, there is no doubt; for he does not care for battle, my dear, O you who are skilled in warfare.
t.6.53.11: There is no one of mine who equals you in friendship and in strength. Go forth, O Kumbhakarṇa, for the slaying of the enemies and for victory.
t.6.53.12: The destroyer of foes swiftly seized a sharpened spear, made wholly of black iron, blazing, and adorned with refined gold.
t.6.53.13: That terrible weapon, equal to Indra's thunderbolt, as heavy as the vajra, the destroyer of Devas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas and Kiṃnaras.
t.6.53.14: Taking up his sharp spear, hung with a great garland of red flowers, blazing with fire that sprang from itself, and stained with the blood of his enemies, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words to Rāvaṇa.
t.6.53.15: I shall go alone; let this great army remain here. Today, hungry and enraged, I shall devour those monkeys.
t.6.53.16: Having heard the words of Kumbhakarṇa, Rāvaṇa spoke these words: "Go, surrounded by troops bearing spears and maces in their hands."
t.6.53.17: For the monkeys are high-spirited, swift and resolute; they would bring to destruction with their teeth anyone who is alone or careless.
t.6.53.18: Therefore go forth, surrounded by troops exceedingly hard to overcome, and destroy the entire hostile faction of the enemy, harmful to the rākṣasas.
t.6.53.19: Then the greatly splendid Rāvaṇa sprang up from his seat and fastened upon Kumbhakarṇa a garland interspersed with jewels.
t.6.53.20: He fastened upon the great-souled one armlets, finger-rings and other excellent ornaments, and a necklace gleaming like the moon.
t.6.53.22: Wearing golden armlets and bracelets and adorned with ornaments of gold, Kumbhakarṇa, the huge-eared one, shone like a fire into which oblations have been well poured.
t.6.53.21: Rāvaṇa fastened divine and fragrant garlands of flowers upon him, and set the splendid earrings in his ear.
t.6.53.23: Resplendent with a great dark girdle about his hips, he looked like Mandara bound by the serpent at the churning for the nectar of immortality.
t.6.53.24: As he was being fastened into his golden armor, strong enough to bear any burden, impenetrable, gleaming like lightning and seeming to blaze with its own radiance, he shone like the king of mountains wrapped in clouds at twilight.
t.6.53.25: His limbs bound with every ornament and a spear in his hand, that rākṣasa shone like Nārāyaṇa when he had roused his energy to take the three strides.
t.6.53.26: Having embraced his brother, circumambulated him, and bowed his head to him, the mighty one set forth; Rāvaṇa sent him off with excellent blessings.
t.6.53.27: Amid the resounding blare of conches and kettledrums, chariot-warriors followed that great-souled one, the foremost of chariot-warriors, together with troops bearing excellent weapons, with elephants and horses, and with chariots rumbling like thunderclouds.
t.6.53.28: Mounted on serpents, camels, donkeys and horses, on lions, elephants, deer and birds, they followed that terrible Kumbhakarṇa of mighty strength.
t.6.53.30: And many foot-soldiers followed, rākṣasas loud-roaring and mighty, terrible, fearsome-eyed, with weapons in their hands.
t.6.53.29: Showered with flowers of bright hues, a parasol held over him and a sharp spear in his hand, fierce with intoxication and maddened by the smell of blood, he, the enemy of the Dānavas and the gods, set forth.
t.6.53.31: Red-eyed, of enormous bodies, resembling heaps of dark collyrium, they raised their spears, swords, and sharpened axes.
t.6.53.33: Then, assuming another form, dreadful and hair-raising, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa of great splendor rushed forth.
t.6.53.32: And huge missiles many fathoms long, fit to be hurled and hard to withstand, and huge trunks of palm trees, fit to be hurled and hard to withstand.
t.6.53.34: He measured a hundred bows in girth and stood six hundred bows high; fierce, with eyes like the wheels of a cart, he looked like a great mountain.
t.6.53.35: Having gathered the Rākṣasas together, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa, huge like a scorched mountain and with an enormous mouth, laughed and spoke these words.
t.6.53.36: Today, enraged, I shall burn up those troops of the foremost monkeys one by one, as a fire consumes moths.
t.6.53.38: The root of this siege of the city is Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa; when he is slain, all is slain. I shall kill him in battle.
t.6.53.37: Indeed, the forest-roaming vānaras do me no wrong; that species is the adornment of the city gardens of such as we are.
t.6.53.39: As Kumbhakarṇa was speaking thus, the rākṣasas raised a tremendously dreadful roar, as though making the ocean tremble.
t.6.53.40: As the wise Kumbhakarṇa swiftly sallied forth, terrible-looking omens appeared on every side.
t.6.53.41: Clouds most dreadful, laden with meteors and thunderbolts, roared aloud, and the earth with its oceans and forests trembled.
t.6.53.42: Terrible-looking jackals howled, their mouths filled with mouthfuls of flame, and birds wheeled in circles from right to left.
t.6.53.43: As he went along the road, a vulture swooped down and settled upon his spear; his eye throbbed, and his left arm trembled.
t.6.53.44: Then a blazing meteor fell with a terrible roar; the sun became lusterless, and no pleasant wind blew.
t.6.53.45: Paying no heed to the great, hair-raising portents that had arisen, Kumbhakarṇa went forth, driven by the power of Death.
t.6.53.46: Stepping over the rampart on foot, he who resembled a mountain beheld the wondrous army of monkeys, which looked like a dense mass of clouds.
t.6.53.47: Then those monkeys, seeing that foremost of Rākṣasas, who resembled a mountain, fled in all directions like clouds driven by the wind.
t.6.53.48: Beholding that exceedingly fierce army of monkeys fleeing in all directions like a scattered mass of clouds, Kumbhakarṇa, who resembled a dark cloud, roared again and again like thunder in his delight.
t.6.53.49: Hearing his terrible roar, like the roar of a rain-cloud in the sky, many of those monkeys fell to the earth like sāla trees whose roots have been cut away.
t.6.53.50: Bearing a massive iron club, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa sallied forth to slay the enemy, striking the most dreadful fear into the hosts of monkeys, like the Lord wielding his Kiṃkara staff at the end of the age.
